title: Your Partners Are Already in Salesforce. Use Them.
summary: Pick the object holding your partners, filter for what counts as one, map name and email — and stop re-typing companies your CRM already knows.
body_markdown:
*The slowest part of standing up a partner program is usually data entry for companies your CRM already knows about.*


---


Ask a team how their partner list got into the partner program and the answer is often that somebody exported a view and re-typed it. That has two costs: the obvious afternoon, and the one that matters — **the list is stale the following week** , because new partners keep arriving in the CRM and nothing carries them across.


## The four decisions


Syncing is less a configuration task than four decisions, and getting the second one right is most of the work.


**1. Which object stores your partners.** There is no universal answer: some organizations keep partners as Accounts with a record type, some use a dedicated object. Ask where your own team actually creates a partner, not where the data model says they should.


**2. What filter identifies a partner.** This is the real decision, and the field type matters: a **picklist** gives you the same controlled dropdown Salesforce shows, with no typo risk. A **free-text** field has to match spelling and case exactly — confirm the value with whoever owns your Salesforce data rather than typing what you think it is. A filter that is too loose pulls customers into the partner program; too tight and the partners your team adds next month never appear. The test is not whether the filter matches today’s list — it is whether a *new* partner, created next month by a rep following your normal process, will match it.


**3. Which fields are name and email.** Mundane, and the one that breaks quietly. The email you map becomes how the partner is contacted and invited, so mapping a generic company address rather than a person’s is the difference between an invitation that reaches someone and one that reaches nobody.


**4. Whether documents come too.** Files on your Salesforce partner records can flow into the file library automatically. Worth an explicit decision rather than a default, because partner records often carry agreements and internal notes, and “everything on the record” is rarely what you meant.


## Test before you save


There is a test step before saving, and it is not ceremonial. It answers the only question that matters — *does this filter select the companies I think it selects* — at the one moment when a wrong answer is free.


The failure it prevents is specific and annoying to undo: a filter that is slightly too broad imports a set of customers as partners, and now your partner program has records that should not exist, in a system that other people are already looking at.


## What “stays current” actually buys


The recurring value is not the initial import — it is that **your partner program stops being a snapshot** . A rep creates a partner account in Salesforce the way they always have; it appears in the program without anybody being told to do anything.


That is what makes a partner program survive contact with a growing team. Any process that depends on somebody remembering to copy a record across will drift, and the drift is invisible until somebody asks why a partner has no portal access.


## Frequently asked questions


### Which Salesforce object should store partners?


Whichever one your team actually uses to create a partner today — often Accounts with a record type, sometimes a dedicated object. Match the real process rather than the intended data model.


### How do I choose the filter that identifies a partner?


Test it against the future, not the present. A good filter matches a partner your team will create next month following their normal process, not just the companies on today’s list.


### Which email should I map?


The one you want invitations and notifications to reach. Mapping a generic company address rather than a person’s is the most common reason a partner invitation reaches nobody.


### Do Salesforce documents come across too?


They can — files on partner records can sync into your file library. Make it an explicit decision, since partner records often hold agreements and internal notes.


### Why sync instead of importing once?


An import is a snapshot that starts going stale immediately. A sync means a partner created in the CRM next month appears without anyone remembering to copy it.


## Takeaways


- Four decisions: the object, the filter, the field mapping, and whether documents follow.
- **The filter is the real work** — judge it by whether it will catch next month’s partner.
- Map a person’s email, not a generic company address.
- Use the test step. A too-broad filter imports customers as partners, and that is unpleasant to undo.
- The point is not the first import; it is that the list stops being a snapshot.
